sections.h2: Does Kansas tax capital gains when you sell a house?
sections.html:
Yes. Kansas starts from your federal adjusted gross income, so any gain the IRS counts flows into your Kansas return. Kansas law (K.S.A. 79-32,117) builds Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI with listed modifications, and the Department of Revenue's estimated tax worksheet begins with total adjusted gross income and then applies one rate schedule to taxable income. It shows no separate capital gains line.

That means the first question is the federal one: is any of the gain taxable at all? If the IRS lets you exclude it, the excluded amount never reaches your federal AGI, and so it does not reach your Kansas return either.

Sellers often mix up the sale price with the gain. The tax is figured on the difference between what you realize from the sale and your adjusted basis, and a loss on a personal home is not deductible, according to IRS Topic 409.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the federal home sale exclusion?
sections.html:
If the house was your main home, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, when you meet the ownership and use tests. IRS Topic 701 sets out the rules.

  • Ownership test: you owned the home at least 24 months out of the 5 years before the sale.
  • Use test: you lived in it as a residence at least 24 months of those same 5 years. The two periods can fall at different times.
  • Joint returns: either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • Repeat sales: you generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home during the prior two years.
  • Reporting: if you receive a Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when the whole gain is excludable.

People on qualified official extended duty in the Uniformed Services, the Foreign Service or the intelligence community can elect to suspend the five year test period for up to 10 years.

sections.h2: What federal rates apply to a gain you cannot exclude?
sections.html:
For 2025, most net long-term capital gain is taxed at no more than 15% for most people, with 0% and 20% bands on either side. A gain is long-term when you held the home for more than one year; one year or less makes it short-term and taxes it as ordinary income.

These are taxable income thresholds, and anything above the 15% ceiling is taxed at 20%. IRS Topic 409 also notes a maximum 25% rate on unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property, which can matter if you depreciated a rental, and it points to the net investment income tax for higher earners.

sections.h2: How much Kansas tax does the gain add?
sections.html:
Kansas uses one schedule for taxable income. For tax year 2025, a single filer pays 5.2% on the first $23,000 and $1,196 plus 5.58% of the excess above that; joint filers use $46,000 as the break point and $2,392 as the base. The 2025 standard deduction is $3,605 for single filers, $8,240 for joint filers, $4,120 for married filing separately and $6,180 for head of household.

A quick illustration using those numbers: if your total Kansas taxable income after deductions came to $50,000 as a single filer, the tax would be $1,196 plus 5.58% of $27,000, or about $2,703. This is arithmetic from the published schedule, not a prediction for your return.

Kansas has passed further rate cuts. The Department's Notice 25-06 describes future income tax rate decreases, so check the booklet for the year you sell instead of relying on the 2025 figures.

sections.h2: Can you adjust your Kansas basis?
sections.html:
Kansas allows a subtraction where your Kansas adjusted basis is higher than your federal basis, limited to the gain included in federal AGI. The statute is K.S.A. 79-32,117(c)(iii).

Basis is generally the cost of the asset. For a house you inherited, IRS Publication 551 says basis is generally the fair market value on the date of the owner's death. An heir who sells soon after inheriting can end up with little or no gain, which is why a date-of-death appraisal is worth ordering. Our page on the Kansas estate and inheritance tax covers the inheritance side.

If you sold under a contract that spreads payments across years, you made an installment sale, and the IRS says you report it under the installment method unless you elect out. The home exclusion stays available either way.

sections.h2: What if you live outside Kansas but own a Kansas house?
sections.html:
The gain is still a Kansas matter. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) says capital gains and losses from sales of real property located in Kansas are allocable to Kansas, and the Department's partnership booklet states that a nonresident owner is subject to tax on gains realized from the sale of property located in Kansas.

For estimated tax, the Department says nonresidents should consider only Kansas-source income when testing the conditions. You must make payments if your expected Kansas tax after withholding and credits is $500 or more and your withholding may fall short of the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax.

  • 2025 voucher dates: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15, 2026.
  • Payments go to Estimated Tax, Kansas Department of Revenue, PO Box 3506, Topeka, KS 66625-3506, or online through the Kansas payment portal.
  • The Department's taxpayer line is 785-368-8222.

sections.h2: Which forms report a Kansas house sale?
sections.html:
On the federal side, you calculate the gain on Form 8949 and summarize it on Schedule D of Form 1040 when a report is required. A Form 1099-S from the closing agent triggers reporting even if the gain is fully excluded.

If the sale produced a loss on a personal home, it is not deductible. If you hold other capital losses, the net amount you can use against income in a year is limited to $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the excess carried forward. A taxable gain may also require federal estimated tax payments, which IRS Topic 409 ties to Publication 505.

On the Kansas side, the number you carry over starts from the federal return, so errors made in the federal calculation repeat on the state return. Keep the closing disclosure, the improvement receipts and the exclusion worksheet together for at least as long as the return could be questioned.

sections.h2: How should a Kansas seller plan for the tax?
sections.html:
Work out the basis and the exclusion before you accept any offer, because those two numbers decide whether a tax bill exists at all. A cash buyer does not change the arithmetic, since the rules above turn on basis, ownership and use rather than who writes the check.

Gather the closing statement from your purchase, receipts for improvements, and any appraisal or tax records that help fix the date-of-death value for an inherited house. A tax professional can tell you whether a sale late in the year, or a payment under an installment contract, changes which tax year the gain lands in.

faqs.q: Is there a special Kansas capital gains rate?
faqs.a: The Department of Revenue's worksheet shows no separate capital gains rate. Gain flows into Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI and is taxed on the standard schedule, which for 2025 is 5.2% and 5.58%.

faqs.q: Do I owe Kansas tax if I exclude the gain on my federal return?
faqs.a: Generally no, because excluded gain is not part of federal AGI, which is where Kansas begins. You still report the sale if you receive a Form 1099-S.

faqs.q: How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?
faqs.a: You need to have owned and used it as your main home for at least 24 months out of the 5 years before the sale. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months.

faqs.q: Does a nonresident owe Kansas tax on a Kansas house sale?
faqs.a: Yes. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) allocates gains from Kansas real property to Kansas, and the Department states nonresidents are taxed on gains from Kansas property.

faqs.q: What is my basis if I inherited the house?
faqs.a: Generally the fair market value on the date of the previous owner's death, per IRS Publication 551. A few exceptions exist, so read the publication or ask a tax professional.
